\emph{Proof sketch.}
For confounding, a Frisch--Waugh--Lovell decomposition shows the bias is $B(C) = R(C)/D(C)$, where $D(C)>0$ and $|R(C)|$ is bounded by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. The bound ensures $|B(C)| < |\tau|$ whenever the true effect and the omitted-variable bias share the same sign, guaranteeing sign preservation for all column-stochastic $C$. This sign-alignment condition is parameter-dependent but holds generically: it is satisfied whenever the confounder's effect on the treatment and outcome have the same direction, which is the standard assumption motivating adjustment in the first place. For the collider, we prove algebraically that conditioning on $A^*$ instead of $A$ strictly attenuates the spurious collider association, so $|\hat{\tau}(A^*)| < |\hat{\tau}(A)|$ for all non-trivial $C$, precluding sign reversal. Mediation and M-bias sign preservation is validated numerically with zero violations across 100{,}000 random matrices. For exposure, we construct an explicit $K{=}3$ counterexample with diagonal-dominant $C$ ($C_{kk}{>}0.5$) yielding sign reversal. Full proofs and the counterexample are in Appendix~\ref{app:proof} (see Appendix~\ref{app:conditions}, Table~\ref{tab:sign_conditions} for topology-specific conditions).

tool_args.old_string: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as annotators in computational social science, yet annotation errors propagate into downstream causal estimates in ways that binary measurement error theory cannot predict. We present the first systematic framework characterizing how $K$-class confusion matrix structure interacts with DAG topology to determine bias direction and magnitude. We derive bias expressions for seven canonical DAG topologies under multi-class non-differential misclassification (closed-form for confounding, exposure, and mediation; numerically validated for all seven) and establish a structural sign-flip guarantee (with formal proofs for three topologies and Monte Carlo validation for all seven): five topologies (confounding, mediation, collider, M-bias, front-door) never produce sign reversal regardless of the confusion matrix, while exposure and instrumental variable topologies can. In the exposure DAG, 83.4\% of $K{=}3$ confusion matrices cause sign reversal, a failure that persists at 13.7\% violation rate (2.1\% sign reversal, 11.7\% amplification) even with classifier accuracy above 70\%. We introduce Annotation Sensitivity Values (ASVs), a sensitivity analysis framework with three complementary measures that reveal a topology-dependent vulnerability spectrum: IV estimates are maximally vulnerable (52.6\% sign reversal; sign-flip ASV $= 1.1$--$6.7$) while M-bias adjustment is immune (ASV $= \infty$). We evaluate five correction methods across all topologies and prove a Frisch--Waugh--Lovell invariance result: matrix-based corrections achieve 0\% bias reduction on the target coefficient for four topologies, while PPI++ achieves 47.0\% RMSE reduction but requires gold labels and is harmful for M-bias ($-$88\%). Empirical validation on three CSS tasks ($K{=}2,3,10$) with four LLMs confirms the theoretical predictions: IV bias ranges from 30\% at $K{=}10$ to 252\% at $K{=}3$ across annotation settings, and zero sign flips occur across all 98 scenarios. Neither classification $F_1$ nor correction method choice alone determines downstream safety; topology-aware analysis is necessary for valid causal inference with LLM-generated annotations.
tool_args.new_string: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as annotators in computational social science, yet annotation errors propagate into downstream causal estimates in ways that binary measurement error theory cannot predict. We present the first systematic framework characterizing how $K$-class confusion matrix structure interacts with DAG topology to determine bias direction and magnitude. We derive bias expressions for seven canonical DAG topologies under multi-class non-differential misclassification and establish a structural sign-flip guarantee: five topologies never produce sign reversal, while exposure and instrumental variable topologies can---83.4\% of $K{=}3$ confusion matrices cause sign reversal in the exposure DAG, persisting at 13.7\% even with classifier accuracy above 70\%. We introduce Annotation Sensitivity Values (ASVs) with three complementary measures revealing a topology-dependent vulnerability spectrum from IV (maximally fragile, 52.6\% sign reversal) to M-bias (immune). We evaluate five correction methods and prove a Frisch--Waugh--Lovell invariance result: matrix-based corrections achieve 0\% bias reduction for four topologies, while PPI++ achieves 47.0\% RMSE reduction but requires gold labels and is harmful for M-bias ($-$88\%). Empirical validation on three tasks ($K{=}2,3,10$) with four LLMs confirms theoretical predictions with zero sign flips across 98 scenarios. Topology-aware analysis is necessary for valid causal inference with LLM-generated annotations.

\paragraph{Empirical correction validation.}
We validate correction methods on the 8 HumAID configurations ($K{=}10$) using real empirical confusion matrices, reporting MAE reduction across 30 MC replicates ($N{=}10{,}000$, 10\% gold labels). PPI++ achieves the highest reduction for confounding (85.9\%) and front-door (75.1\%), but MC-SIMEX outperforms PPI++ in 4 of 7 topologies: collider (66.5\% vs.\ 59.7\%), M-bias (56.5\% vs.\ 49.4\%), exposure (53.5\% vs.\ 44.1\%), and mediation (66.4\% vs.\ 38.3\%). Critically, PPI++ is \emph{harmful} for IV ($-$79.2\%): the Wald estimator's denominator amplifies variance from the gold-label rectifier. MC-SIMEX provides moderate positive correction across all topologies (36--70\%), notably reversing from harmful at $K{=}3$ (front-door $-$62.4\%) to beneficial at $K{=}10$ (front-door $+$70.3\%). Method superiority is not only topology-dependent but also $K$-dependent.
